utterances.text: I don't -- this meeting with Mr. Tomovic, as far as I could remember his name, lasted not too long and as I told you there were not circumstances to provide, to conduct any interview with this witness, and I don't believe that I share any information with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't, but why was it short, sir, and why were you not prepared? Did it just be a happenstance that you ran into him or did you call him in advance and schedule a meeting with him days, if not weeks, prior to you coming to his home to interview him?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is very simple, we didn't know. As far as I remember, we didn't know where the witness lives and where he's located. I just took the chance that I was driving from Sarajevo to another place, maybe to Zvornik or Bratunac. I don't remember right now where exactly but I stopped in Han Pijesak and I phoned this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, at any time since those two interviews in Han Pijesak, the first one, and Sarajevo, the second one, did you get in contact with Mr. Beara's driver?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not personally. It's possible that I called him but I don't remember right now. I called him to show up for this interview in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about after the interview in Sarajevo is really what I'm getting at, sir?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. After the interview in Sarajevo, I never was in touch with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And do you think, sir, by failing to refresh a witness's recollection such as Mr. Tomovic with either the vehicle log documents or other documents or statements from other witnesses, that it would be a breach or a violation of your professional, ethical and legal duties as the lead investigator in the Srebrenica case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Ostojic, there was the first occasion when the witness confirmed that he met with this person at his residence in Han Pijesak. And if I have understood the witness correctly, there was no proper interview then. It was just a first meeting, mostly intended to confirm that he had been found and that there will be a second interview later on, date of which will be communicated to him. Second instance was the Sarajevo interview at which, if I understood the witness well, he doesn't even recollect being present. So he cannot confirm or deny any of the suggestions that you are putting. So the conclusion, according to me, is in regards to the first instance, you cannot allege a failure to show the gentleman logbook, notebook or whatever it is. As regards the second instance, you also cannot suggest failure to the witness because he's not in a position to answer you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I see the Court's point and thank you. But, Your Honour, I would like to just clarify that first meeting if I will. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can clarify the first meeting without suggesting any undue -- because he's told you that there was no proper -- no proper interview then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd also object, Your Honour, that my friend is misstating the facts as he's putting it to the witness. I think he knows that there is no legal, ethical and professional obligation to show one witness another witness's statement which he knows that and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's another matter. That's another matter and I wouldn't ask the witness to answer that because he is not -- he is an investigator and not a lawyer. Unless you are a lawyer and we don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think we have the witness's testimony on what he feels his personal, professional obligations as well as ethical obligations, I just find it hard to believe that the Prosecutor is taking that view. But in any event, Your Honour, I have a couple more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, is it true what our honourable Mr. President said that that first meeting was just an introductory meeting and that you didn't ask any questions but just wanted to confirm where the driver of Mr. Beara was?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him what will be the -- what will be the issue for the proper interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you prepared an information report, did you not, based on that contact that you had with Mr. Beara's driver?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should look up this information report. I don't remember this information report right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, to the best of your recollection, sir, is it your testimony here under oath that you did not ask any questions of Mr. Tomovic in connection with the events in July of 1995 involving Srebrenica but merely obtained general information as to his telephone number, address, where will he be living in the next few days until you could obtain contact from him, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I asked him a few questions about the events in 1995, but as I told you, that was not circumstances to conduct an interview. It was at his accommodation in the presence of his family. I didn't want to discuss these events with him in the front of his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so that I understand because I did read the information report, sir, but based on your recollection when you say a few questions, how many did do you think you asked him?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, don't ask me right now. I would prefer to look at my notes and information report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all I have, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Is there re-examination, Mr. Nicholls? I hope not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. Ostojic for keeping within the 30-minute limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First, very briefly, Mr. Blaszczyk, you were asked about investigators under your command in this team. Do you command investigators in the OTP?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am not. As I told you, maybe I didn't express properly but I am the most experienced investigator in this team, I mean Srebrenica team. This is why I am so-called leading investigator but I am not responsible, I am not supervisor of other investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we put 2967 up in e-court, please? While that's coming up that's the statement of Nebojsa Vukicevic which has been asked about. And back when he was first cross-examining you, Mr. Ostojic stated that the collection according to this statement was in Zvornik for one year from April 1998 through March of 1999. And I can make this quick because I think my friend might agree with me that it doesn't say anything like that in this statement and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We did discuss it, Your Honour, and we clarified it after he objected on the 22nd of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this statement, to continue, it was read out to you, parts of it, about -- if we can scroll down, the keys being given to Dragan Obrenovic, once the -- once the documents were transferred to Mali Zvornik. What kind of institution were they held in in Mali Zvornik, what sort of place was it?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the premises of Defence department of Serbia, the military premises of Serbia and Montenegro, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And from your reading of the statement, does the statement say or imply that Mr. Obrenovic, as Mr. Ostojic put it to you, had the sole access and was the only person who could get the documents in a military facility in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go now and show you P192. That's a document Ms. Fauveau asked you about at T 18114 to 16 and let me just check if we still have the original here. I'll wait for that to come up on e-court. While we are waiting, I'll remind you that you referred to, I think, you called it a binder of documents that you saw in Zagreb. Okay, could I have the assistance of the usher, please? I'm going to hand you some original documents. Please show it to my friend, first, Mr. Ostojic, or Ms. Fauveau. Now, can you -- first of all, tell me if you recognise what I've just handed to you, that packet of paper with a cardboard cover?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this small binder. At that time when I saw this binder, it was clipped together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was going to ask you about that. What do you mean by clipped together? I see that there are holes punched in the cardboard cover and also in the pages.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents were clipped together and this is the first page, this is cover page of this small binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, could you turn to what should be the last page in there, 04258580? Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. When did you first see that document?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am very sure, 100 per cent sure, that I saw this document first time in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I'll just ask this question although it's quite clear. When you saw this document in Zagreb, was it -- how did it get to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document arrived to Zagreb together in -- yeah, with other documents from so-called Drina collection from Banja Luka, on 17 December 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm done with that. And just can you remind us - if you can read it - what is written on the cardboard cover of that binder?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's mean telegrams and the number of the telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they quote the name of Atlanti Dabat [phoen]. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked some questions by my friend Mr. Ostojic and by Ms. Fauveau about who had access, in fact that was a huge part of your cross, who had access to the Drina Corps collection while it was in Mali Zvornik. And what I'd like to do now is show you some documents and I spoke to my friends about this which we received from the Krstic Defence. And the first is 2979. This is a receipt from 19 February 2000 to the Office of the Prosecutor, re receipt for disclosure of materials Prosecutor versus General Radislav Krstic and it's signed by senior trial attorney Mark Harmon. For the moment, could I just ask you to take a look at numbers 4, 20 and 23, these documents we received in February 2000?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you scroll down, this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll have to go to the next page. Now I'd like to go to an exhibit which is in evidence, P00927. And to save time if we look at this, we'll see that it's a Main Staff VRS document number 03/4-1670, 17 July 1995, and this is document number 4 on the list of documents received from the Krstic Defence. We'll need to look at the Serbian originals. And I'll ask you to take a look when you can as well at the stamp and small amount of handwriting on the document, at the bottom. Now, if possible, if we can keep that up on the screen, I'd like to put on 2982, the Serbian original, next to it. While waiting for it to come up, we'll see that that is also Main Staff RS document 03/4-1670 of 17 July 1995. And could we go up to the top, please, sorry, of the -- of 2982? We see that ERN number 04257985, is that a -- well, what collection does that come from?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the ERN number, I see that these documents comes from Drina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we see, can you just look at the numbers handwritten on the top right-hand corner of both documents, the one we received from the Defence and the one we received from the Drina Corps collection and tell me if they look similar?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look down at the stamp and the handwriting --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe we have the originals of each of these here in case anybody wants to look at it. Well, we have the original from the Drina Corps collection, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you look at those two stamps, and the handwriting, written in the stamps, the date, do they appear -- does one -- is the one on the left 0927, appear to be a photocopy of the original 2982?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to now put up, please, 2981 and if possible next to it 2982. This is a Drina Corps command document number 04/156-9 from 10 July 1995, and this is number 23 on the list of documents disclosed in Krstic. I'll just wait for those two to come up, please, next to each other. I think we've got the wrong one on the right. It should be -- the ERN should be 04367235. Yeah, 2980. Maybe I misspoke. That was the one I wanted on the right, sorry. And here, if we can scroll down towards the bottom of both documents, and look at the stamp and the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems that one of these documents is original and other one is a copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now can we go up to the top, please? Again, 2980 is the document on the right, with the ERN number 04367235. What collection does that ERN number signify that this document came from?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is Drina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The last two, it's same exercise, if we could have up 2745 on the left and 2983 on the right. This is another command of the Drina Corps document 03/156-11, 13 July 1995. Number 20 on the Krstic Defence disclosure receipt. And when you've looked at those if we could scroll down again to the stamps and the handwriting, compare these two, please. And could we scroll down to the bottom, please, so that we can see the stamp and the signatures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we do the same with -- okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems the same documents, one of them is original and another one is copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, I'm sorry, if we go up -- well, on the right we have the ERN number 04312743.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a range of Drina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, is it 2743? What we are -- maybe that is the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 43 to 44, you're correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that your answer, the same?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is a range of Drina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, again, we received these documents in February 2000, the copies on the left we've been looking at. Did the OTP know where these Drina Corps documents were at that time or have access to them?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's all I have, Your Honour. I'll just say that my understanding is that these documents received from the Krstic Defence were the result of -- and I can't speak to an official request make to the Republika Srpska for these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Blaszczyk, we don't have any further questions for you, at least for today, so you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wish to thank you for having taken the trouble to come again and I hope we will not disturb you any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just wondering whether we now have two separate series of documents that you wish to tender, which I suppose is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct. Miss Stewart has combined them on one list but has indicated which testimony they are pertinent to and which testimony they came in with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then we can do that now. Because if you are not prepared for that, I was going to suggest to have the break straight away during which you would sort it out. Where is the list? Have the Defence been provided with a copy? Not yet. So I think it would be appropriate to have the break now so that each Defence team has got time to go through the list, because otherwise, I can't expect anyone to be in a position to decide whether to object or not to object. We'll have the 25-minute break now. Do you want to explain anything from this -- no, I think it's self explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour, perhaps is not completely self-evident. 2985 is the English transcript of the -- what's been referred to as the raw material shot by Zoran Petrovic that we watched in court with the road book testimony. That transcript is also the one which we saw synced to the video, video V0006747. If you look at the transcript, the cover sheet explains that the two versions of that video were used to make the transcript because some portions were clear, some unintelligibles could be heard on the BBC copy that could not be heard on the copy we received from Mr. Petrovic and vice versa. And so where language comes from the BBC as opposed to the raw material we copied from Mr. Petrovic during our interview that is indicated in the transcript so that one can see which video is used for that particular portion of speech and translation. And in addition, there is a key to the abbreviations used for unidentified male, unidentified female, and the main speakers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. We'll have a 25-minute break now and then we'll process these documents, as well as the Defence ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've had time to go through the Prosecution list of proposed documents to be tendered in relation to the two matters that the witness testified upon on different occasions, one being the Drina Corps collection and you have nine documents there on direct, and seven on redirect, and then the road book, seven and five, 12. Any objections, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would object to the tendering of documents P20805 [sic] through 2813 through this witness, because these nine documents, in providing of these documents, this witness did not take part, either from Yugoslav or Republika Srpska authorities. His only role in -- is in the second repacking of these documents in Zagreb from 24 to 57 boxes and also he did not participate in receiving of these documents in The Hague where the photos were -- where the documents were unpacked and photos were taken. Finally, he did not make inventory of these documents. On the other hand, not a single person participating in the process testified before this Trial Chamber. Some of them provided witness statements, but not called to testify under oath and cross-examined by the Defence. Consequently, due to gap in providing and due to gap in our knowledge about places where these Drina Corps documents were for five years from 1999 to 2004, we cannot establish what documents were taken, replaced or added to the Drina Corps archives and because of that, I object to tendering of these documents through this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll join in that objection, Your Honour, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just with respect to the second portion of the documents, and I'm not sure if you covered it and I apologise, if he had, the Petrovic video, we would make the same or similar objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I believe that Mr. Blaszczyk laid a perfectly adequate foundation for all these documents to be admitted. He had personal knowledge of all these documents, he may not have been the person who actually received some of these but he laid the foundation through his work in the OTP, through his knowledge of the way that the documents were received, the correspondence, the official reports from the Republika Srpska, and his actions in the chain of custody once the documents came to Zagreb to -- and then came to us. He was intimately involved in the way these documents came. The focus of my direct examination obviously was the chain of custody once the OTP became aware of these Drina Corps documents and once the OTP took possession of them in Banja Luka. That's what all of these documents were referred to. The argument about who had access to these documents earlier has nothing to do with the admission of these exhibits and I think that Mr. Blaszczyk has demonstrated to the Court that these are authentic documents, that they are probative and they're reliable and therefore they should be admitted. And most of my friends' arguments I think go to the weight, not to admission, because the admissibility has been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. For the purpose of admissibility we are talking of relevance and probative value, and nothing else. Of course, some areas like you mentioned of authenticity are by-products of probative value and also of relevance sometimes. All right. I need to confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Setting apart some of your submissions, Mr. Zivanovic, with which we don't need to deal with because there is a standard set for admissibility purposes at this stage, our position is that we unanimously come to the conclusion that these documents on a prima facie basis meet those standards and they are therefore being admitted. Then obviously at the end of the exercise we will give them all the attention that they deserve. All right. We also have some Defence documents from the Miletic Defence team. These have been circulated, three documents, 5D434, 5D432, and 5D533. Any objections from your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any objections from the other Defence teams? So they are so admitted. Then I do have another list of -- from the Borovcanin team but I think that belongs to the second issue. All right. So yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I mention for completeness the Trial Chamber very kindly gave me a few days to consider the documents that were put to General Nicolai in re-examination, particularly bearing in mind I'm told they are going to be dealt with with a witness who is coming next week, I don't think he's protected but I won't give his name, I've got no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. So Madam Registrar, you know what we are talking about and you'll deal with that. Thank you, Mr. Josse. We now -- is there any other Defence team that wishes to tender documents in relation to the first part of Mr. Blaszczyk's testimony, namely that relating to the Drina Corps collection and the recovery thereof? None. So we move to the second matter that the witness testified upon, namely the so-called road book. As I said I think there are 12 documents that the Prosecution seeks to tender. Are there any objections? I heard before Mr. Ostojic challenging. Yes, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Just given the witness's testimony in connection with the road book evidence, in fact, I think it's clear so I won't recite it, I think it would be inappropriate to introduce this evidence through this witness given that he just verified some pictures and wasn't the person actually who conducted and prepared the documentation in connection with that and the video presentation that he presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's not a ground for objection, I don't believe. If I understand the objection, it's just that he physically didn't select all the exhibits, the photos and put them together. Mr. Blaszczyk made it very clear that he worked with a person with more technical expertise to create the CD presentation, and also the printing of the book. We don't need to call the person who hit all the computer keys when Mr. Blaszczyk was there explaining where to put various photos. We don't need to call the person who worked on putting the book together and binding it. He made clear that his knowledge of these -- of these photos, exhibits and documents and again as Your Honours rightly said, the issue is whether it's probative and relevant when we seek to introduce evidence and I think we've gone beyond a prima facie showing of relevance for all the documents we seek to tender relating to the road book testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to make sure that you're both on the same wavelength and that we equally are fine-tuned with you. Which of these 12 documents in particular were you objecting to, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To all of them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All of them, okay. All right. Any further objections from other Defence teams? None. I need to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our position is exactly the same as before, Mr. Ostojic. We appreciate, of course, your submission and that will be taken into consideration at the right moment. But the standards set by the rules and by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal for the admission of documents at this stage in our consideration is met and therefore these documents are hereby being admitted. Then there is a Borovcanin Defence team list of three documents, they are all 4DIC and that's 194, 195 and 196. These are colour photographs, photographs that have been marked by the witness. I take it there are no objections on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't imagine there are objections from any other Defence team. None. So these three documents are so admitted. Is there anyone else who wishes to tender any other documents from the Defence teams in relation to the second part of Mr. Blaszczyk's testimony? None. So that closes the Blaszczyk testimony for the time being. Are you ready with the next witness, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, we are ready to proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's call him. We have three-quarters of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, please put your ear-phones on because I need to address you. First of all, I hope you understand that the reason why you have been waiting is because we had a previous witness that took a little bit longer than we expected, and so, please accept the Trial Chamber's explanation and apologies. You're here to give evidence and our rules require that before you do so, you make a solemn declaration that you will be speaking the truth. The text is being handed to you. Read it out and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So help me God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You still have to put the ear-phones otherwise we will have problems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The reason, Mr. Petrovic, I would imagine if I speak loud enough and if others speak loud enough, you will be able to hear but as we go along, there are comments made by the interpreters, if there are words that they haven't understood, words that they need to you repeat, and you won't be able to follow unless you have the ear-phones on. I mean, I know they are uncomfortable but believe me we have to stay here every day with -- for over three and a half hours with them so I can understand that they are uncomfortable. But be patient with us and we try to get over and done with this testimony as soon as we can. Just let me explain a few more things. I heard you speak in French.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Partly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll be speaking in English, for example, and others may be speaking in Serbo-Croat or in French. I would like to know first and foremost when it comes to interpretation, which language you wish to receive. We can provide you with English, French or your own languages, which is Serbo-Croat. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it I am informed that you have the floor channel which means that you will be able to follow the proceedings in whichever language they are being conducted, say if I'm speaking in English you would be receiving me in English now. I want to make sure that you understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And French obviously you understand otherwise you wouldn't be speaking it and your own language I have no doubt you understand. So do you wish, I see that you wish to address the Trial Chamber before you start giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First and foremost, I decided to speak French for a very personal reason, but I shall speak Serbian afterwards. This had been agreed with Mrs. Carla Del Ponte's office as well as Defence lawyers. In order not to complicate matters, I wish to address myself to you directly before we start, just for a few minutes because these are to me, this is vital to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has to do with a letter I addressed to you. I explained to you why I could not be here before today. There are two things, I can clarify, and I can only clarify this with your assistance so I would like you to help me in this. Because of the report I prepared, that is the reason why I am here today. I have suffered for years in Serbia. This is not something very important to you here but I do not live in The Hague and I don't live in Paris and I don't live in Malta. I live in Belgrade. So it so happens as I told in the letter that a former employee of the ICTY, Mr. Ruez, caused me a lot of problems in my country. But he never actually met me, which is even more serious, I believe. When he conducted his research work, he said or he concluded or he said he could not infer whether I was a journalist or a policeman. Given the regime we were living under, this, I believe, is a greatest offence you can commit. This has been recorded in the official documents of this Tribunal, I think as part of the Krstic case, and will remain there forever. Another point I would like to clarify with Mr. McCloskey today, and I hope we will be able to settle this issue, because it is very similar to what Mr. Ruez has said. In other words, I was a so-called journalist, as you say in English, and what was said in 2006, before this Tribunal, was not, Mr. McCloskey, not very accurate. And in Serbia, one has a feeling that I had been sent by Belgrade, when you say Belgrade that means the Belgrade regime that had sent me to prepare this report which you have been using for a number of years. I am not very spoilt. I've done a lot of things in my life. But this is something which I cannot accept, and I cannot forgive anyone if nobody apologises, if nobody tells me outright that this is wrong. I have been asked to be honest, I have been given a letter, Mr. McCloskey did, and I think this issue was cleared up, and I'm grateful to him for that. But there is the office of Mrs. Carla Del Ponte and I cannot accept that even though I am not such a resourceful person, I cannot live with that so I would like you to settle this issue very quickly. It's not very complicated to do. Mrs. Carla Del Ponte's office can also say something. But if somebody has not understood me, I recommend you to read Avishai Margalit, the Israeli philosopher's book, entitled, "The decent society." That is the driving force behind my speech today. The last thing I wanted to say but which is very important if you set it against the backdrop of Serbia, I -- for some unknown reason, all the lawyers and various departments of this Tribunal avoided me. My pictures have been used extensively. There were a lot of so-called experts and I'm the greatest so this was quite clear in General Krstic's trial and nobody called me before 2002. Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin who asked me to come and testify to talk about what I saw whilst I was shooting this video, and I accepted this on moral grounds. I know that the witnesses here are neither in favour of one or other party so to speak but over there, it is very important for me to be able to say that the reason why I was asked to come -- I was asked to come, and it was Mr. Borovcanin asked me to come and I want everybody to know this in Serbia. I'm sure you will understand what I'm saying. It doesn't matter, I was without a witness to begin with and I want my people to help me and I want my people to know about this. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Petrovic. Let me explain just a couple of things before we proceed. It's true that you sent a letter addressed to us directly following the issue of the subpoena. I conceded at the time that you were unaware, as most people are, that it's not regular procedure, not a regular practice to write directly to the Chamber, to the Judges, but there is a special procedure that one needs to follow, failing which basically it is the duty of the Judges to not only to ignore that letter but to send it over to the registrar who would then communicate with you and explain to you that you cannot do this, this is wrong, et cetera, et cetera. We didn't even do that because reading through the letter, we understood that this was not a frivolous letter that you were writing but you were justifying, trying to justify that your failure to attend previously was not motivated by any contempt towards the Tribunal but because of personal reasons that you had and which you wanted to make known to the Trial Chamber. So I think that explains to you why you did not get a response from the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber is not expected to act except in one way and we didn't even act that way, not to embarrass you and not to create problems for you. And I hope you understand now what happened. The other thing is the complaint you have against Mr. Ruez. I think the only person who can provide or create a remedy is you yourself now, that have been given this golden opportunity to have your day in court where you can explain why you disagree completely with what was stated about you by Mr. Ruez in the past. And you will have every opportunity to do that, even if no direct questions are put to you on the issue. The third thing, and which you complained about the way you were described in this trial by Mr. McCloskey, I think, has been cleared by Mr. McCloskey in a most dignified manner. And I do wish to express our appreciation for the way you did this, Mr. McCloskey, because it was the right and fit thing to do in the circumstances. Asking us, however, to intervene with Mrs. Del Ponte's office or with her personally to deal with the rest, which is more or less related to what was stated by Mr. McCloskey is beyond what we can do. And I would suggest to you, you seem to be a very reasonable and sensible person, with whom we can have a healthy exchange while your testimony progresses, I think I would suggest to you that you consider that when Mr. McCloskey expressed his regrets and provided you with an explanation, that was not only his own personal position that he was taking. He doesn't come into this courtroom and make a representation on his own behalf. He represents Mrs. Del Ponte, and her office, that is the Prosecutor of this Tribunal. So if there was an apology, I would suggest that you also take it as an apology from the office of the Prosecutor and not merely as one forthcoming from Mr. McCloskey himself. And I hope that satisfies you and that we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for understanding. We will certainly not finish your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you and I do accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But I could understand. This is the complication. I can follow you in French. So I got the interpretation after I had already understood what you had stated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can go to speaking the Serb language, if you wish. I said in French what I wanted to say, so to accelerate matters, I can now go into Serb. I was listening to you in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you can -- you have to keep it because, for example, sometimes I receive comments that you were running too fast, for example. You wouldn't know that were you running too fast so you need to keep the headphones. It won't be of any help to yourself and to us if you remove them. We will spend --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can speak whichever language you choose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will follow you in English, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. And you can then speak and intervene in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will be translated to us because we don't understand the language. Okay. So we can now start the procedure. It's going to be like this. Mr. Nicholls for the Office of the Prosecutor is going to go first. He is expected to last about two hours, I take it. He will then be followed by the various Defence teams, and it's estimated we are in the region of about three hours all of them put together. I also wanted to tell you one thing, since you mentioned something about the Defence teams that they have ignored you, they haven't shown you any importance, et cetera. It's not the case. I can assure you that whenever we have discussed you or your report here, that was done with the utmost respect both from the Prosecution and from the Defence counsel. So please put your mind at rest that you enjoy all the respect and if we notice that anyone shows disrespect to you, we will intervene and protect you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Nicholls. We'll finish at 7.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The first thing I want to ask you about is your background. Then I'll ask you a little bit about how you know Mr. Borovcanin. And then the third thing I'll ask you about is, as His Honour put to you, for you to explain in your own words how you came to travel to Srebrenica and Potocari and film this footage. So we'll get to that quite soon. First of all, could you tell us your full name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: My nickname is Pirocanac because there it's like John Smith in England and America. Zoran Petrovic is John Smith, so everybody knows me by my nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you just tell us what the nickname means, if it does mean anything?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think it -- nomen est omen. It means that my parents came from this region near Bulgarian border. This is a town Piroc and Pirocanac is a man from Pirot, Pirotian, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Belgrade, 30 of August, 1953.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how long have you lived in Belgrade or are have you lived --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: All my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Whole life, okay. Can you tell us about your -- just a little bit about your education and then your professional background as a journalist. What -- briefly give us a run through of your career.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I graduated at the philological faculty of Belgrade, French literature and language. I did my post-graduate studies, my master in -- at Paris university, Ecole des hautes etudes en sciences sociales, one of the prestigious schools in France. And I am just about to finish my PhD at the same school. This was one very important reason for which I couldn't satisfy your needs before. So I'm employee of the Institute of Political Studies in Belgrade which is a state-run institution. And in this institute, I lead a small centre for geopolitical studies which is called southeast Jugoistok in Serbian. So I am, I could say, an expert in geopolitics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us a little bit about your work as a journalist and whether that was primarily as a reporter, if I use the right word, or whether you also worked as a cameraman in the past before 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I started in famous Belgrade student weekly, Student, which gave, we can say best journalist in ex-Yugoslavia. So in -- but practically started with the mainstream media in 79, I was for six months in Nicaraguan war, covering events in Nicaragua. I went two more times. So my career was mostly world policy subjects connected with the hot spots in the planet. So I did a lot of reports from Israel, I was in Lebanon in 85, I was kept and captured for 40 days by some tough group. So I have a long experience in difficult subjects. And I covered also events in civil war in Yugoslavia, in ex-Yugoslavia, Vukovar, Sarajevo, Majevica, Semizovac, Srebrenica; so I covered most of the important events. Mostly I worked during the war for French television, TF1, which is the biggest private television in Europe, and I was most of my career independent journalist. I was the first, if I can say, independent, freelance journalist from the communist world ever in this foundation, Journalistes En Europe in France which was founded by the founder of Le Monde, Hubert Beuve-Mery, and I am very proud of this moment in my CV. So mostly I couldn't get full employment in Serbia. I worked and my best years were in Croatian magazine Star which was best-ever magazine in Yugoslavia. So I was known for at least 20 years from now as a known journalist, as le grand reporteur, as the French say. So I'm just for three years permanently employed and I'm nearer to my retirement than to the beginning, much nearer. So -- but this is a society we lived in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you some questions about Mr. Borovcanin, and if -- could you start by telling -- excuse me, when you first met Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, I will start now in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: For other people. [Interpretation] I met Mr. Borovcanin for the first time, if I recall correctly, in 1994, in the winter of 1994. There was a large offensive. A telecommunications system was supposed to be taken over at Mount Majevica close to the Serbian border. I wanted to make a reportage for the telegraph weekly published in Belgrade. If the interpreters believe I'm going too fast, by all means they should warn me. I appreciate their work and I know that most people speak too fast. It was an exceptionally interesting situation for a journalist to be in since a group of Serb soldiers was surrounded at the top of the mountain where the telecommunications centre was, and it was one of the key points for telecommunications links in the whole of Yugoslavia. This was the crossroads of TV, communication networks, a very sensitive spot. And I asked to go and report from there. I didn't know that I would meet Mr. Borovcanin then. Together with a group of their soldiers, I climbed up the mountain in deep snow. It was very difficult to get through the encirclement. Fire was opened upon us and the same applied to when we were going back a week later. Why was it interesting for me? I learned that some Mujahedin were there, volunteers from the Muslim countries, and I personally saw them there in close proximity of the Serbian positions. Those are the guys yelling Tekbir, Tekbir, and are fierce and fanatical fighters. The reportage was published, including the cover page, and it was a scoop for me. As far as I recall, perhaps I met commander Saric, I'm not certain because they didn't go all the way up to the summit. I didn't go with them. I went with a group of soldiers. A year later, perhaps a bit over one year, in 1995, in the summer of that year, three to four weeks before the events in Srebrenica, I located them again and I wanted to take some footage for Studio B, although at that point, or subsequently, I never received a camera from that poor TV station. They had one camera and they needed it in the city in order to cover the events there. That -- the case referred to here and the camera I'm talking about is also something I had at Semizovac when we went with Ljubisa Borovcanin to reach their positions; they were in a double ring of encirclement. They were encircled from the outside and from the inside by the Muslims, and to cover a few hundred metres as the crow flies we had to take the round about way of some 80 kilometres. That is why some footage may be too long but I know that Christiane Amanpour, at the time, made a report with the Black Swans which was a special unit of the Bosnian army. And there were a number of Islamic volunteers there as well. I wanted to do the same but she has a team of 10 to 15 to work with. Those people of Mr. Borovcanin's helped me that I showed the conditions they were in living in the forest and at the positions. The broadcast was actually called, "When you catch a fox alive." And the third meeting was concerning Srebrenica, when I established contact with that unit from Belgrade. I asked for him, although I wasn't able to locate him right away. Then he called back. It was probably on the 12th of July. I had certain doubts as to the date, whether it was the 12th or the 13th or the 13th and the 14th. However, we agreed that it was probably the 13th and the 14th. Thanks to the date you can see on the footage itself. It was long expected that Srebrenica would fall. It was expected to happen for months and all the world agencies were reporting on that and that's why I wanted to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go back a bit and ask you a couple of follow-up questions and then we'll get to July. The campaign at Mount Majevica, if I pronounce it correctly, how long did you spend with Mr. or Commander Borovcanin at that time in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly. I was at the staff, down there. I don't know what the place was called. And I probably saw him there with Saric. In any case, I know I saw General Saric first, in the reportage, General Saric figures as a more important person than Mr. Borovcanin. But I don't remember we had any particular contact then. Maybe I was wrong. Maybe I just saw him at the command then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: In any case, his team, his elite unit, permitted me to go there at my own risk all the way up to the summit. I was embedded. They covered me, tried to have me not get killed, but that was basically their task. I was quite lucky.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So let me just -- I think this is clear but let me just make sure. When you were with Mr. Borovcanin's unit in 1994, you were embedded, as you say, that was during -- you were with them while they were in actual combat; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I climbed up to a group of soldiers, maybe 50 strong or perhaps up to 100, they were defending the relay point which is strategically very important. All around there were Mujahedin, and I know that, for example, when I left the house, I was followed by their doctor and was -- who was wounded in the leg by the Muslim soldiers. It was quite tough. The news report was published. Had we discussed this earlier, you would have been able to find it in the Telegraph. It was five or six pages long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just very briefly how long were you embedded with that unit, with Mr. Borovcanin's unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I climbed up to the top -- well, maybe two or three days, I believe it was in March, maybe you can see it in the newspaper. There was a great snowstorm, bad weather. I was there during the time I needed to make the news report, take some photographs and then descend. It was quite an effort for them because they had to enter the besieged area and then leave it again. It's always a risk to have soldiers wounded. However, I believe I justified their trust and efforts since I produced a balanced report that I'm proud of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if could you please tell me -- you started to talk about this and I asked to you stop for a minute -- about how you came to meet with Mr. Borovcanin in July 1995 in Bratunac, the process first of who you had to ask for permission or what you had to do to be able to go and report on the events in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I managed to do that with a very state-of-the-art device called telephone, since it was in another country in Republika Srpska. I was in Serbia and when on the 11th of July all news agencies of the world announced that Serbs entered Srebrenica, in the world of journalists it is madness because everyone wants to be there from all over the world. By the way, when I was there, there were dozens of different journalists, but no one asked them to talk about it. Maybe they might be of assistance, people such as Mr. Block from England or a photographer from the US. They came there with NGOs as usual. There was this excitement among the journalists, there were dozens of them from Serbia, and all over. And on the 12th, since I initially failed to contact those people, I set out towards the border crossing called Ljubovija, there is a bridge over the Drina River. I tried to cross it with my passport and with my press ID, however, unsuccessfully. They told me that operations were on going, Serbs had entered Srebrenica but battles were going on for a while after that. I returned to Belgrade and during that day, in the evening, I believe, I managed to convey my message to Mr. Borovcanin's unit and he called back. The credit which I had earned objectively reporting on their unit was probably decisive. The next day, he waited for me at the bridge, at which I had not been able to pass the previous day, and then we entered Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you just tell me very briefly what -- how you explained to Mr. Borovcanin what you wanted to do and what you wanted to accomplish by going to Srebrenica and what he said to you about being able to come and work with his and be with his --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can you repeat the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, it's not a good question. What did Mr. Borovcanin say to you during that telephone conversation when he called you back?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I truly do not recall the conversation. However, I know that we discussed that I couldn't cross. I must have told him that I tried on the 11th and the 12th to do that. I tried to get into touch with the press service of Republika Srpska as did other Serbian journalists but we were all told not to come. We were -- we are a small country, a small village, so to say, we all know each other and someone told me, Pirocanac, don't come here. I don't know whether it was a Colonel. In any case he told me, don't come here; we would have to arrest you since operations are still ongoing. The same situation as in Iraq, if you are not embedded with US troops, it is impossible for you to enter as a journalist. That was the situation. I don't remember any other details. I do remember, however, that I tried to persuade him to help me to see what was going on. He agreed right away. He could have said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And thank you. This conversation was on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Maybe it was 11th, I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you started to say how you met Mr. Borovcanin at the bridge in Bratunac. Best as you recollect, what day was that that you met Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: The 13th of July. I don't know the day now. I should look to the calendar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: But it was 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And best as you remember, about what time was it that you met on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, [Interpretation] There was a procedure. You first had to cross the Serbian border and then the border into Republika Srpska on the other end of the bridge. In any case, since a lot of time has passed, I can go by the first scene that you can see in my report, when I arrived at the Dutch compound. It was around 2.30 or perhaps around 3.00. I think the first time recorded is 14 hours 29 minutes. Perhaps the procedure took some half hour at the bridge. I don't think it is very important. In any case, I entered Bratunac and the compound around 2.30 or 3.00, as far as I recall. And this can be checked against the recording, the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. We just have a few minutes. I've got a couple other questions before we break for the day. You recall you met with me for the first time on 28th of February in Belgrade in our field office there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: 6, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And also with me was Mr. Blaszczyk, my investigator?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Blaszczyk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Zoran Lesic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Employee, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Employee with the --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sound was not so well at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And on that day, do you recall that you provided us with a copy of your raw footage from the 8-millimetre tape that you had, the original tape you had used in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you recall signing -- that we asked to you sign the tape and you were -- excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This whole series of questions were leading ones. Obviously. My colleague is putting his -- well, his assertion to the witness asking him to confirm. So he knows the way how to ask questions. I think it would be more proper because it's examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that, Your Honour. I frankly didn't think this was a matter where I would be getting an objection but I don't -- should I just -- I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: After you gave us the copy of your 8 millimetre tape and we copied it on our equipment, did we ask to you do anything with that tape?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Strictly speaking, you're right, Mr. Lazarevic but it's more practical to proceed the way Mr. Nicholls was handling the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't hear well the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's simple. Do you recall that you signed the tape for us, the copy that you --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: I signed several things among this cassette also.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, now, the copy that we made from the tape you brought to the interview, what was the tape that you brought to the interview, your 8-millimetre tape? Was that an original recording or was that copy of a copy of a copy or something?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, I gave I think already before to Mr. McCloskey, if I remember, to his crew, VHS cassette of the disappeared original 28 minutes programme documentary Operation Srebrenica that I found finally in Canada, if you believe or not, because the original disappeared from Studio B. Until today nobody explained how it was possible because, as I know, it is the only in the history of 20 years of Studio B, only original programme made which disappeared. It was on the cassette which was called Umatic. It's not any more in use, very big, and it disappeared I was told from Studio B from the bureau of the editor-in-chief. So -- but I was lucky that some Serbs in Canada kept this cassette so this is one material. And you are talking about our meeting and this was my cassette, original, with some slight changes. I think today I don't know what happened for everything which was there but I was happy when my -- my VHS copy reappeared to explain a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll ask you a couple more questions about that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we can, Judge, this would be a good time for me to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's perfect. Mr. Petrovic it's time to stop here today because our time is over. You will have time to relax because we will be sitting tomorrow in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say -- as this is the end of the day, if you will entitle me to be a little bit cynical in French. As I have spent over four hours up top there, there was very cold breeze up there. It was a bit claustrophobic. I'm not a softie but I couldn't help thinking that this is what happened when people were deprived all the time and there was air coming in all the time. I hope I don't have to wait four hours tomorrow again, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow we will start immediately with you at 2.15 in the afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Merci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
